It’s our mission to provide a safe and healthy environment in which families and businesses will thrive. We are committed to fostering community pride, building relationships through neighbors helping neighbors, and providing a safe place for children to play and grandparents to enjoy their retirement. Our goal is to continue to provide excellent public safety, and municipal services to encourage growth and prosperity for all of our community.
Citizens Engagement Form
If you see a problem in town that needs addressed, please use the following link to report it.
Tree Limb Disposal
Tree Limbs can disposed of two different ways. One way is you can burn them if you adhere to the burn ordinance. The second way is to bundle them up for Heavy Trash pickup, which is the 1st pickup of each month. The tree limbs will only be picked up provided they are tied in bundles not exceeding 4 feet in length and 3 feet in girth.
Pay your bill online
PAY UTILITY BILLS ONLINE - Payments made online will not reach our business office for 24-48 hours. If you have been shut off please contact the office at 317-535-7500 to have your payment processed immediately. WELCOME TO ICMS
Kim Davis, Middle School Principal
It is my privilege to welcome you to our school community. At Indian Creek Middle School, we believe in engaging every student, every day in quality learning opportunities. Our dedicated staff strives to create opportunities for students to be creative, challenged, and collaborative. We are incredibly proud of the opportunities we offer outside of the classroom for students to grow as well. Students have a wide range of extra curricular activities that include Robotics Club, FFA, State Champion Academic Teams and the middle school musical to name just a few.
As Principal, I have spent the last nine years in the NHJ School District. This year promises to be one to remember with our construction projects nearing completion and new facilities opening for our students. We are all looking forward to putting our expanded campus to use and seeing our students shine on the stage and on the court. JOHNSON COUNTY Department of Planning and Zoning (317) 346-4350 86 West Court Street www.JohnsonCounty.in.gov Franklin, Indiana 46131 Courthouse Annex MEETING AGENDA Johnson County Board of Zoning Appeals May 26, 2026, 7:00 PM Public Auditorium, West Annex Building 86 West Court Street, Franklin, Indiana CALL TO ORDER ROLL CALL APPROVAL of MINUTES Meeting minutes from the April 28, 2026 meeting PUBLIC HEARINGS CONTINUED PETITIONS None. Noah Hale.5832 N 75 W, Whiteland VARIANCE OF USE of the Johnson County Uniﬁed Development Ordinance to provide for an HVAC contractor shop, warehouse, and office (not permitted on agriculturally zoned property). OLD BUSINESS None. NEW BUSINESS June Board of Zoning Appeals Meeting Date In accordance with American Disabilities Act, any person attending the public meeting in need of reasonable accommodations in order to attend, hear, or present evidence at the public meeting on an agenda item should contact the Johnson County ADA coordinator, Barb Davis, at 86 W. Court St., Franklin, IN 46131, (317) 346-4329, bdavis@co.johnson.in.us. REPORTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS None. ADJOURNMENT The next regular meeting of the Johnson County Board of Zoning Appeals is scheduled for Tuesday, June 23, 2026, at 7:00 PM. (Virtual meeting information on next page) LIVE STREAMING AVAILABLE HERE Meeting ID: 870 6549 8518 Passcode: 100889 (Link can also be found on the County Website under Events Calendar – Click on Events Website) Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-04-26 ADDRESS: 5835 N 75 W, Whiteland Section 20, Township 13, Range 4 PETITIONER: Noah Hale REQUEST VARIANCE OF USE of the Johnson County Zoning Ordinance to provide for a HVAC contractor shop, warehouse, and offices (not permitted on agriculturally zoned property). VARIANCES OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS of the Johnson County Zoning Ordinance to: 1. Waive commercial parking requirements (paved surface, curbs, and stall striping), 2. Waive landscaping requirements (landscape buffer 20 feet in width), and 3. Allow for a wall sign not to exceed 50 square feet in area. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This 8.63-acre site is zoned AG (Agricultural) and is improved with a single-family dwelling, three accessory structures, and a pool. There are similarly sized parcels to the north and south of the subject site. All are improved with single- family dwellings and various accessory structures. One of the parcels to the north houses a church. The parcel immediately north of the property’s barn is 0.47 acres and is improved with a single-family dwelling. To the west there is a subdivision with smaller parcels. To the east is Proctor Park, a public park owned by the Town of New Whiteland. VARIANCE OF USE This request, if approved, would allow for the subject property to continue to be used as HVAC contractor shop, warehouse, and office. The heating and air conditioning business, Reve Porter, has operated on this site since its establishment in 1979. A variance (V-45-85) was approved in 1985 for the installation of a 100-foot tower for a wind-generating system on the parcel. The windmill is still present on the site. In 2021, the current property owner sought out similar variance that the petitioner is requestion that was approved. The submitted Plan of Operation, included in this staff report, indicates that the business will be open Monday-Friday from 7:30 am to 5:00 pm. The applicant anticipates 9 employees onsite per day and 2 customers per week which is not expected to significantly impact current traffic. There will be one dumpster on-site. No hazardous materials will be stored on-site. The petitioner has not indicated any plans for growth. Per the Zoning Ordinance, the purpose of the AG District is to accommodate agricultural operations and practices.. No businesses directly abut the subject parcel, but there are multiple religious institutions and other businesses in close proximity as the subject parcel is directly west of the Town of New Whiteland’s city limits. Noise generated by vehicles, people, and other business activities is not expected to impact the enjoyment of nearby residential properties. The office has not received any complaints or comments on the current business operating at this location. Staff, therefore, recommends approval of this request. VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS – COMMERCIAL PARKING & LANDSCAPING This Variance of Development Standards request, if approved, would allow for commercial use at this location without providing the paved maneuvering and parking areas required of commercial properties. The petitioner proposes, in 2-5 years, to construct a 30’x50’ concrete parking lot for employees that will not have curbs or stall striping. The lot behind the existing barn is not currently paved. The lack of curbs, striping, and completely paved surfaces does not meet the required off-street parking standards of the Zoning Ordinance and thus requires the variance. The site would be accessed from the existing concrete driveway from 75 W. The parking lot will also be in deficient of the perimeter landscaping requirement. VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS – WALL SIGN This request, if approved, would provide for the future placement of a less than 50 square feet non-lit wall sign on the west side of the barn. The Zoning Ordinance prohibits business/commercial signage at a agriculturally-zoned parcel. FINDINGS OF FACT: VARIANCE OF USE 1. The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. Staff Analysis: The current business does not alter the traffic patterns on 75 W. Approval of the variances would not impact the general public. The business would have limited on-site customers. Construction of the barn and pavement additions would require building permits and compliance with all building codes before passing final building inspections. 2. The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will be affected in a substantially adverse manner. Staff Analysis: Indoor storage of business equipment and materials would allow the appearance of the property to remain consistent with neighboring properties. The distance from other properties, fencing, and trees on the site create visual barriers from the right-of-way. 3. The need for the variance arises from some condition peculiar to the property involved. Staff Analysis: The petitioner purchased the property with the proposed use already occurring. The petitioner is applying for the variances to legally establish the use that has been occurring since 1979. 4. The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will constitute an unnecessary hardship if applied to the property for which variance is sought. Staff Analysis: The property has been used commercially for over 40 years. The current structures, proximity to the Town of New Whiteland, other commercial uses, and residential subdivisions make it less desirable for agricultural use. 5. The approval does not interfere substantially with the Comprehensive Plan. The Future Land Use Map of the Comprehensive Plan indicates Suburban Residential as the future land use of the property. The proposed use is less intense than permitted agriculture uses and is consistent with other uses in the surrounding areas. STAFF ANALYSIS OF FINDING OF FACTS - DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS VARIANCE State Requirement: The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. Staff Analysis: The current business does not alter the traffic patterns on 75 W and Tracy Rd. Approval of the variances would not impact the general public. The business would have limited on-site customers. Construction of the barn and pavement additions would require building permits and compliance with all building codes before passing final building inspections. State Requirement: The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will not be affected in a substantially adverse manner. Staff Analysis: The existing barn and proposed addition would provide space for indoor loading, unloading, and storage of business equipment and materials. The onsite dumpsters are not visible from the right-of-way or surrounding properties due to fencing and the size of the lot. The majority of the parking areas on site are paved, excluding the area immediately behind the barn which is gravel. Therefore, the appearance of the property would remain residential, which would not necessitate the need for landscape buffers for screening purposes or completely paved parking areas. The wall signage will be a low impact to identify the business. State Requirement: The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will result in practical difficulties in the use of the property. Staff Analysis: The property could not maintain a residential appearance without a variance from paving and landscaping requirements. GENERAL INFORMATION Applicant: Noah Hale 32 Morningside Ct Whiteland IN 46184 Owner: Holden Properties LLC 5835 N 75 W Whiteland, IN 46184 Zoning: AG (Agricultural) Land Use: Commercial and Residential Future Land Use: Suburban Residential -MNH V-04-26 BASE MAP Subject Site V-04-26 BASE MAP II V-05-26 AERIAL V-04-26 BIRD’S EYE VIEW V-04-26 SITE PLAN V-04-26 PLAN OF OPERATION V-04-26 PETITIONER’S FINDINGS OF FACTS – USE VARIANCE V-04-26 Site Photo – Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-05-26 ADDRESS: 6709 S 200 W, Trafalgar (parcel #: 41-11-19-034-021.000-020) PETITIONER: Jeffery and Emily Bradley by Van Valer Law Firm LLP REQUEST VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS of the Johnson County Zoning Ordinance to allow for a 1,360- square-foot accessory dwelling unit (a maximum of 1,000-square-foot accessory dwelling is permitted). PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This 32.48-acre site is zoned AR (Agricultural Residential) and improved with a residential home and a couple accessory structures. The property is surrounded by smaller-sized parcels used residentially. VARIANCE REQUEST This variance request, if approved, would allow for an accessory dwelling with a building area of 1,360 square feet. This property was once the Indian Spring Golf Course, which has not been in operation since 2014. The property owners have converted the property back to a residential homestead with farming activities. There is a structure on the building that the petitioner wishes to convert to an accessory dwelling. The structure is currently 1,360 square feet in size. There is no attached garage or storage space. The Zoning Ordinance states a maximum of 1,000 square feet of building area for an accessory structure. The creation of accessory dwelling standards was intended to allow an opportunity for property owners to provide care for a family member, or to provide accommodation for visiting family or friends, which is generally considered a benign secondary use of residential. A 1,000 square feet is an adequate living space to achieve the intent to provide care for a family member while encouraging independent living. FINDINGS OF FACT: VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS 1. The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. The second dwelling will not impact public health, safety, morals, or general welfare, as it will be verified that it is built to local and state building codes. 2. The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will not be affected in a substantially adverse manner. The structure in question has been established and integrated into the fabric of the neighborhood for close to 50 years. Because its footprint and presence are long-standing, it represents a permanent, recognized component of the local landscape rather than a disruptive new addition. 3. The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will not result in practical difficulties in the use of the property. The petitioner has failed to demonstrate that there are unique physical circumstances or conditions particular to this specific parcel of land—such as irregular lot shape, exceptional topography, or pre- existing infrastructure—that prevent them from adhering to the established development standards for an accessory structure. 4. The variance is not primarily for the economic benefit of the petitioner. While economic benefit is present with this variance and could be a secondary consequence, it is not the primary motive need for the variance. 5. The variance request is a minimum deviation that is needed to be awarded to the applicant. The request involves an addition of only 350 square feet beyond what the ordinance allows. Because this addition utilizes a structure that has already been established and integrated into the property for close to 50 years, the expansion represents the minimum necessary deviation to adapt the existing footprint for its intended purpose. 6. The variance request is due to hardship caused by the current owners of the property. The pursuit of a non-conforming design means the hardship is one of choice or preference, not one inherent to the land itself. GENERAL INFORMATION Applicant: Van Valer Law Firm LLP 225 S Emerson Ave Suite 181 Greenwood IN 46143 Owner: Jeffery and Emily Bradley 6709 S 200 W Trafalgar, IN 46181 Current Zoning: AR (Agricultural Residential) Existing Land Use: Agricultural – Residential Future Land Use: Rural Residential -MNH V-05-26 Base Map V-05-26 Base Map II V-05-26 BIRDS EYE VIEW Accessory Dwelling V-05-26 STREET VIEW Accessory Dwelling Primary Dwelling V-05-26 FLOOR PLAN V-05-26 Petitioner’s Findings of Facts

NEW BUSINESS None. REPORTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS None. ADJOURNMENT The next regular meeting of the Johnson County Board of Zoning Appeals is scheduled for Tuesday, July 28th, 2026, at 7:00 PM. LIVE STREAMING AVAILABLE HERE Meeting ID: 870 6549 8518 Passcode: 100889 (Link can also be found on the County Website under Events Calendar – Click on Events Website) Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-07-26 ADDRESS: 5362 Warrior Trail, Whiteland, Parcel #: 41-05-23-041-023.000-033 PETITIONER: Sandhu Properties INC, By Chad Leinart REQUEST VARIANCE OF USE of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance to allow for a trucking parking and trucking facility business (not permitted in a GB zoned property). PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This variance request involves a 12.696-acre parcel zoned GB (General Business). The property is currently unimproved, though it contains an existing dwelling that is not being used for residential purposes. The land is currently being utilized for parking. Surrounding land uses include: South: Several semi-tractor oriented businesses. North: Semi Parking, Warehouse, and manufacturing uses, including a similar use approved in 2023 by the Board of Zoning Appeals. All affected parcels, with the exception of 5440 Warrior Trail, are located within the Town of Whiteland limits VARIANCE OF USE REQUEST If approved, this Variance of Use request would allow the property to be redeveloped as a commercial truck parking lot, with the potential to repurpose the existing structure for fleet operations. Proposed Site Plan & Operations Parking Capacity: The submitted site plan proposes parking for approximately 71 semi-trucks and semi-trailers. Structure Reuse: The existing structure is proposed to be converted into an office building. Technical Review Adjustments: The final number of parking spots may be reduced during the Technical Review Committee (TRC) review of the civil plans to ensure compliance with development standards, including parking lot setbacks, landscaping, and drainage requirements. Hours of Operation: According to the petitioner’s submitted Plan of Operation, the facility will operate 24 hours a day with security. REGULATORY REQUIREMENTS The development will be required to go through the Technical Review Committee process and must adhere to the following:  All commercial standards in the zoning ordinance.  Procurement of a State Design Release for commercial use of the existing building.  Full compliance with all requirements of the Stormwater Management Ordinance. STAFF NOTES AND RECOMMENDATION This property has been continuously used for truck parking without authorization from staff, despite repeated enforcement notices from the department. However, staff notes that this formal application indicates the property owners are now making an effort to correct past violations and establish a compliant parking facility. If approved, this process will ensure the development is better suited for the area in both appearance and operational use. The existing dwelling on the property has previously been used by the property owner and guests as a social gathering spot, which has presented ongoing issues for the Town of Whiteland. The house is currently unfit for occupation. This unauthorized use must cease immediately, regardless of the outcome of this variance request. The Town of Whiteland has provided an official response to this use request, which is attached to this staff report for review. The requested variance is consistent with and similar to the uses of adjoining properties. Staff recommends the following conditions for consideration: 1. Required Approvals: The development must obtain all required permits and approvals before any improvements are made to the property. 2. Cease Existing Operations: All current semi-truck parking on the property must be removed until proper permits have been issued and site improvements are completed. 3. Structure Occupancy: The existing structure cannot be occupied or used until proper commercial permits have been obtained. 4. Nuisance Mitigation: If the structure is not brought into commercial use within one (1) year of this approval, it must be demolished and removed from the property to deter improper use and prevent a public nuisance. 5. Town Interlocal Agreement: The development must include and adhere to all stipulations provided by the Town of Whiteland. STAFF VARIANCE OF USE FINDINGS OF FACT: STAFF ANALYSIS 1. The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. The proposed conversion of the property into a secure, 24-hour commercial semi-truck parking facility will not be injurious to the public health, safety, or general welfare, provided all staff conditions are met. The property will undergo a rigorous Technical Review Committee (TRC) process to ensure proper drainage, stormwater management, landscaping, and setbacks are implemented. Furthermore, requiring the unapproved, hazardous use of the existing residential structure to cease and mandating its removal if not developed within one year directly mitigates an existing public nuisance and improves community safety. 2. The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will be affected in a substantially adverse manner. The proposed use is highly consistent with the established character of the immediate area. The property is bordered to the south and north by semi-tractor-oriented businesses. By bringing this site into compliance through formal development standards, the physical appearance and operational safety of the site will be significantly upgraded compared to its current unauthorized state, thereby protecting adjacent property values. 3. The need for the variance does arise from some condition peculiar to the property involved. The 12.696-acre parcel is currently zoned GB (General Business), which does not permit the transportation and logistics support uses that have become dominant in this immediate area. Due to the intense semi-tractor traffic and industrial warehouse operations directly bordering the site to the north and south, it is highly impractical for this property to be developed for any of the retail or light commercial uses standardly permitted in the GB district. The unique physical location of the parcel—effectively locked within a heavy industrial and transportation corridor—creates a distinct peculiarity where standard general business uses are no longer viable or compatible. 4. The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will constitute an unnecessary hardship if applied to the property for which variance is sought. Strict adherence to the GB zoning text would restrict the property from fulfilling its most logical economic use as a support facility for the surrounding transport sector. Forcing standard retail or office development on a site locked between semi-truck facilities and manufacturing warehouses creates an unnecessary hardship, as such businesses would struggle with compatibility. Granting the variance allows the petitioner to formalize and legally rectify the land use in a way that matches the market reality of the corridor. 5. The approval does not interfere substantially with the Comprehensive Plan. The Comprehensive Plan’s recommendation for mixed use in this area. Mixed uses development is intended to encourage a well-planned, integrated mix of compatible uses that relate well and support one another. This use is compatible with other uses in the area. GENERAL INFORMATION Applicant: Chad Leinart 3200 Sycamore Ct, Ste 2A Columbus IN 47203 Owner: Sandhu Properties Inc 5362 Warrior Trl Whiteland IN 46143 Zoning: GB Land Use: undeveloped land, parking Future Land Use: Mixed -use ~MNH V-07-26 Base Map subject site V-07-26 Base Map II V-07-26 AERIAL Proposed Plan of Operation, V-07-26 V-07-26 Petitioner’s Findings of Facts 6/11/2026 Members of the Johnson County Board of Zoning Appeals Re: V-07-26 Sandhu Properties INC 5362 Warrior Trail The Town of Whiteland (TOW) has been made aware of the request for a use variance for the property located at 5362 Warrior Trail, which is located in Johnson County. • Warrior Trail, which is owned by the Town of Whiteland, is only designated for 11,000 lbs and is not designated for truck traffic from 790’ north of Whiteland Rd. to the end of Warrior Trail. The road that was put into place for the neighboring parcel at 5440 Warrior Trail was regulated to have no more than 35 trucks. The road has been installed less than 18 months, and that portion of the road is already failing. With an already failing road, adding additional trucks will only add to the problem that has been created by the previous trucking development. See attached photos that were taken on June 9, 2026. • Stormwater. This site, since 2020 has increased impervious surface with no regards to any type of improvements on drainage. • IDEM/County Drainage Board/Municipal permits. As they have seemingly changed the overall layout of the property, have they ever obtained any permits for the improvements that have been made on this parcel? Have they ever reached out to the local jurisdiction for any type of official improvement or inquired about what would be required of them? • The TOW police department has made numerous interactions on this property, and it has created a nuisance in the general area due to exterior condition of the property. This has been a blighted property within our community since the parcel owner has taken ownership. • The increase in truck traffic and the impact that this type of development would have on TOW owned infrastructure would not outweigh the positives that would come from this parcel. They would undoubtedly utilize the existing structure as an “office” but would but would continue to utilize in the same condition and occupancy it currently as a multi-family structure. The Town of Whiteland is concerned that allowing this type of development would ultimately lead to more issues and resources being utilized by our staff than the positives that would come from this type of development where there is already a litany of viable options with parcels to the south to allow for trucking facilities and truck parking. We kindly request that this variance be denied, due to the state statute requirements for being granted a use variance based on IC 36-7-4-918.4 which requires: 1. “The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community” - This would disproportionally represent the injurious portion to the Town of Whiteland as we have had multiple police resources and code enforcement regarding trash and rubbish in the area. Adding to the additional issues we’ve already seen with the neighboring parcel, this would only add additional trucks and usage on the TOW infrastructure. 2. “the strict application of the terms of zoning ordinance will constitute an unnecessary hardship if applied to the property for which the variance is sought” - Purchasing a property with an intent that does not allow a permitted use of a zoned parcel does not constitute an “unnecessary hardship” rather a lack of planning on behalf of the parcel owner. Based off the Johnson County’s planning department definition within the current UDO states an “unnecessary hardship” Significant economic injury that: a. Arises from the strict application of zoning regulations in this ordinance to the conditions of a particular, existing parcel of property; b. Effectively deprives the parcel owner of all reasonable economic use of the parcel; and c. Is clearly more significant than compliance cost or practical difficulties. Furthermore, the existing structure doesn’t meet the setback requirements for GC zoning in the current UDO which requires front setbacks based off road designation (Collector/Local-40’, Minor Arterial-50’, I/Principal Arterial-60’). If the BZA does approve the use variance we would request the following commitments by the property owner: 1. Improve Warrior Trail with concrete from the Town limits to the end of Warrior Trail. The Town of Whiteland will be submitting for a Community Crossings Matching Grant program this Fall for reconstruction of Warrior Trail from Whiteland Rd to end of Town limits. This road will be converted to all concrete to ensure that it can withstand the truck traffic. 2. Apply for Town of Whiteland curb cut permit Sincerely, Carmen Young Billy Patrick Town Manager Building Commissioner Town of Whiteland Town of Whiteland Cc: Richard Hill, Whiteland Town Council President Derek Cox, Whiteland Town Marshal Warrior Trail (Photos taken 6.9.2026) Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-8-26 ADDRESS: 2729 Hurricane Road, Franklin PETITIONER: Cara and Andrew Wagner REQUEST VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance to provide for the construction of a 3,424 square foot accessory structure, where all accessory structures will total 4,844 square feet in building area, (The zoning ordinance allows aggregate accessory structure area to be no more than 100 % of the building area of the primary dwelling, or, in this case, 2,642 square feet). STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends the approval of this variance request. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This 2.82-acre site is zoned SR (Single-Family Residential) and is currently improved with a single-family dwelling and two accessory structures. The surrounding land uses include:  North & West: Parcels of a similar size, all utilized for residential purposes.  East: The Legends Golf Club.  South: A planned housing development located within the City of Franklin. The properties directly to the north, south, and east are located within the municipal limits of the City of Franklin. VARIANCE REQUEST – DEVELOPMENT STANDARD The applicant is requesting a Variance of Development Standard to allow the construction of a 3,424-square-foot accessory structure on the property. The site currently contains two accessory structures, an 850-square-foot structure used as a photography studio (previously approved via a Variance of Use) and a 570-square-foot detached garage. With the addition of the proposed 3,424-square-foot building, the total aggregate area of the three accessory structures would be 4,844 square feet. This exceeds the square footage of the primary dwelling, which is 2,642 square feet. The local zoning ordinance stipulates that the total aggregate area of all accessory structures cannot exceed 100% of the square footage of the primary dwelling. This structure will replace an old barn that was removed in 2025. The barn was 1,326 square feet in size. When evaluating variance requests for oversized accessory structures, the department typically considers three evaluation factors. Staff’s analysis of these factors for the subject property is detailed below: 1. Context & Density  Standard: The subject lot is located in a rural or agricultural area, or an area generally characterized by large lots and open, expansive spaces.  Analysis: While municipal expansion and nearby city development have increasingly surrounded this property, the site originally existed in a rural context and retains its large 2.82-acre footprint. The immediate area functions as a rural-residential pocket. Therefore, the property layout can comfortably absorb the physical footprint without creating a crowded or overly dense appearance. 2. Area Consistency  Standard: The subject lot is located in an area where oversized accessory structures are common.  Analysis: There are no other large accessory structures in the immediate area. However, because the subject tract is significantly larger than standard suburban lots (2.82 acres), it possesses the unique capacity to accommodate a larger structure without negatively impacting the neighborhood's pattern of development. 3. Visual Impact  Standard: The oversized accessory structure would be obscured from view from surrounding properties and public rights-of-way.  Analysis: The property is heavily landscaped with mature trees that effectively block the view of the structure from the public right-of-way and a majority of the neighboring residential properties. Conclusion Given that the structure will be well-screened from public view, sits on a substantial 2.82-acre lot, and aligns with the historical and regional presence of large outbuildings, staff asserts that the request represents an acceptable deviation from the zoning ordinance and recommends approval. VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS FINDINGS OF FACT: STAFF ANALYSIS 1. The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. Staff Analysis: The proposed 3,424-square-foot accessory structure will be utilized strictly for purposes accessory to a residential use and will replace an older 1,326-square-foot barn demolished in 2025. It will meet all required building codes and structural safety standards. Because the structure will be placed on a large 2.82-acre lot and used in a manner consistent with residential property management, its construction will pose no threat to the public health, safety, morals, or general welfare of the community. 2. The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will not be affected in a substantially adverse manner. Staff Analysis: The placement of the proposed structure will be to the north, positioned directly behind an existing accessory building. The property is heavily screened by a dense growth of mature trees, which effectively obscures the structure from the public right-of-way and adjacent residential properties. While there are no other large accessory structures in the immediate neighborhood, the substantial size of the subject lot (2.82 acres) ensures that the oversized building will not crowd neighboring properties, diminish their use, or adversely affect adjacent property values. 3. The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will result in practical difficulties in the use of the property. Staff Analysis: The primary residence on the subject property is an older home constructed without an attached garage. In modern home designs, an attached garage is included in the primary footprint, which inherently inflates the allowable aggregate square footage for future accessory buildings. Because this property relies on an existing 570-square-foot detached garage, that space is legally counted against the petitioner’s accessory structure allotment under the strict text of the ordinance. Restricting a large, 2.82-acre tract to standard suburban accessory limits under these specific architectural circumstances creates an unnecessary practical difficulty, punishing the owner for an older layout despite the property having ample physical space to absorb the new structure. 4. The variance is NOT primarily for the economic benefit of the petitioner. Staff Analysis: The requested variance is sought to allow the construction of a storage and personal-use outbuilding to replace a previously demolished barn. There is not economic benefit associated with this request. 5. The variance request IS the minimum deviation that is needed to be awarded to the applicant. Staff Analysis: . The applicant requires a structure of this size to adequately store property maintenance equipment and personal property necessary to manage a nearly 3-acre residential tract. The proposed square footage is proportional to the historical footprint of the property and its physical demands. It represents the minimum deviation necessary to allow the property owner a reasonable level of storage utility that matches the scale of their acreage. 6. The variance request is NOT due to a hardship caused by the current owners of the property. Staff Analysis: The proposed structure has not been constructed without approval, nor have materials been purchased in anticipation of approval. Because the petitioner is seeking formal authorization prior to initiating any development, there is no self-created hardship. GENERAL INFORMATION Applicant: Cara Wagner 2729 Hurricane Road Franklin, IN 46131 Owner: Same Zoning: SR (Single Family Residential) Land Use: Residential Future Land Use: Suburban Residential ~ MNH V-08-26 BASE MAP SUBJECT SITE V-08-26 AERIAL MAP V-08-26 AERIAL MAP II V-08-26 PETITIONER ‘S FINDING OF FACTS

LIVE STREAMING AVAILABLE HERE Meeting ID: 870 6549 8518 Passcode: 100889 (Link can also be found on the County Website under Events Calendar – Click on Events Website) 2 Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-1-26 ADDRESS: 4912 Olive Branch Road, Greenwood 46143 (parcel #: 41-09-32-014-001.000-034) PETITIONER: Darren Poynter, Vickie Poynter by David Gilman REQUEST VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance legally allows a 2,400-square-foot accessory structure, where all accessory structures will total 3,150 square feet in building area. (The zoning ordinance allows aggregate accessory structure area to be no more than 100 % of the building area of the primary dwelling, or, in this case, 1,360 square feet). PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This 0.94-acre site is zoned SR (Single Family Residential) and improved with a residential home and two additional structures. The property is surrounded are similar-sized parcels used for residential on the north side of Olive Branch Road and larger lots used for residential on the south side of Olive Branch Road. Update for July Meeting The petition was continued at the April 28th 2025 meeting with the following motion: To continue V-1-26 to the July 27, 2026 meeting. The motion was based on staff recommendation since construction has not yet commenced and the violation remains on the property. As of July 21st 206, only some site preparation has occurred on the property. On 7/15/26, the property owner provided the following email from their subcontractor From: Cindy Fikes <cindy@mooreconstructionservices.net> To: Vickie Poynter <poynterv@sbcglobal.net> Sent: Tuesday, July 14, 2026 at 02:46:45 PM EDT Subject: Re: E-gress Info Hi Vickie, We are looking at 8/3 to get started on the foundation. I will let you know if we have any weather delays. Typically Daniel Cornett, the Stormwater specialist likes to come out before the digging starts. I will have Ian(Ken refers to him as Wes which is his middle name) reach out to Daniel a few days before we are getting started so he can meet him on site to discuss drainage, concrete clean out bags, etc. Once Brian our concrete guy gets started on the digging, we will coordinate the footer inspection which is when they come out to inspect the holes and make sure they are deep and wide enough before we pour concrete and start to install block. Thank you, Cindy Given the history of this case, the staff recommends that the Board grant a 60-day extension to ensure the property owner fulfills the requirements of the issued permit and shows evidence to resolve the existing violation. Update for April Meeting The petition was continued at the January 27, 2026, meeting with the following motion: 3 “To continue V-1-26 for ninety-one (91) days to allow the Petitioners to present compliant building plans and to remove spoils from the property.” Since the January meeting, the property owner has applied for and was issued a building permit in April for a primary residence addition. Once constructed, this addition will increase the square footage of the primary structure sufficiently to allow for the larger accessory structure currently under dispute. If the addition is completed, the requested variance will no longer be necessary. However, as construction on the addition has not yet commenced, the violation remains on the property. Given the history of this case, the staff recommends that the Board grant a 90-day extension to ensure the property owner fulfills the requirements of the issued permit and show evidence to resolves the existing violation. Regarding the second part of the motion, staff will provide an update at the meeting. VARIANCE REQUEST This variance request seeks approval to classify an existing 2,400-square-foot building as an accessory dwelling, despite it exceeding the maximum allowable square footage for accessory structures on a single tract of land. Under the current Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the total area of all accessory structures is limited to the size of the primary residence. On this specific property, the primary dwelling measures 1,360 square feet. Because there is already an existing 750-square-foot detached garage, the addition of this 2,400- square-foot structure significantly exceeds the permitted allotment. The history of this structure began in June of 2023 when the property owners applied for a building permit for a primary dwelling addition following consultations with county staff. Due to the scale of the proposed project, the owners submitted plans depicting an attached addition rather than a detached building. The design featured a fully enclosed breezeway intended to connect the 2,400-square-foot structure to the main house. However, the connection was never built. As the permit neared expiration, staff notified the owners that failure to construct the breezeway resulted in a zoning violation, as the building remained a non-compliant detached structure. While several options exist to bring the property into compliance, the owners have chosen to seek a variance to bypass the requirement for the connecting breezeway. It is worth noting that when this project was initially permitted, the previous zoning ordinance was even more restrictive, limiting accessory structures to 50% of the primary dwelling's size and requiring that they not exceed the height of the main house. Both the previous and current standards are designed to ensure that accessory buildings remain secondary to the primary residence and preserve the character of single-family developments. Large, oversized accessory structures often fail to blend with neighborhood aesthetics and can inadvertently encourage land uses that are not typically permitted within residential districts. FINDINGS OF FACT: VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS 1. The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. The structure will not impact public health, safety, morals, or general welfare, as it will be verified that it is built to local and state building codes. 4 2. The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will be affected in a substantially adverse manner. This oversizing is inconsistent with the established single-family character of the adjacent properties, there are no similar size structure in the area. A variance of similar requests could be sought by other property owners based on the same findings presented by the petitioner. 3. The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will not result in practical difficulties in the use of the property. The petitioner has failed to demonstrate that there are unique physical circumstances or conditions particular to this specific parcel of land—such as irregular lot shape, exceptional topography, or pre- existing infrastructure—that prevent them from adhering to the established development standards for an accessory structure. The petitioner presented building and site plans that would achieve the standard set forth and attainable. The Petitioner’s findings of fact list the distance and elevation as problematic; the property owner decided to locate the structure in that spot. 4. The variance is not primarily for the economic benefit of the petitioner. While economic benefit is present with this variance and could be a secondary consequence, it is not the primary motive for the variance. 5. The variance request is not the minimum deviation that is needed to be awarded to the applicant. The applicant has failed to present compelling reasoning that the entire amount of the requested variance is essential to overcome the physical hardship. No data was presented demonstrating that a smaller, compliant, or near-compliant structure would not serve the basic intended purpose. Specific justification for the size has not been adequately documented or presented as a necessity that overrides the zoning standard. The request appears to be driven by desire rather than an absolute, physically necessary requirement. 6. The variance request is due to hardship caused by the current owners of the property. The petitioner had reasonable and feasible design options available that would have satisfied the ordinance requirements or substantially minimized the deviation sought. The pursuit of a non-conforming design, despite clear alternatives, means the hardship is one of choice or preference, not one inherent to the land itself. GENERAL INFORMATION Applicant: David Gilman 211 S Ritter Avenue, Ste H Indianapolis IN 46219 Owner: POYNTER DONALD L & POYNTER DARREN E & POYNTER VICKIE L 5035 Cordia CT Indianapolis, IN 46237 5 Current Zoning: SR (single-family residential ) Existing Land Use: Residential Future Land Use: Suburban Residential -MNH 6 Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-09-26 ADDRESS: 378 & 354 Western Blvd, Greenwood & Lot 4 of the Fairview West Commercial Subdivision, Parcel #: 41-03-33-021-027.000-038 and 41-03-33-022-006.000-038 PETITIONER: BLF Acres LLC, By Bill Niemier REQUEST VARIANCE OF USE of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) to allow for the sales, repair, and rental of trailers, truck beds, and golf carts within the Corridor Overlay District (COD), where such uses are prohibited. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION The subject property comprises two lots within the Fairview West Commercial Plat, located east of Interstate 69 (I-69) along Western Boulevard: Lot 3: 2.04 acres, currently improved with a vacant commercial building originally developed in 1997 as a fueling station and restaurant. Lot 4: 3.24 acres, currently undeveloped. These lots are not contiguous and are separated by Western Boulevard. Both lots are zoned GC (General Commercial) and fall within the Corridor Overlay District (COD). Surrounding properties consist of commercially developed lots of similar size and character. VARIANCE REQUEST The applicant proposes to operate a business focused on the sales, repair, and rental of trailers and golf carts, as well as the installation of truck beds. Under the UDO, this activity falls under Automobile/Vehicle Sales, Rental, Service, and Repair. This category is explicitly listed as a prohibited land use within the Corridor Overlay District (COD). Trailers would involve bumper-mounted flatbed, utility, car hauler, and enclosed trailers. It would not involve travel/recreational trailers or boat trailers. Historically, Western Boulevard connected directly to Fairview Road, a major commercial arterial adjacent to former State Road 37. During the conversion of SR 37 into I-69, the Indiana Department of Transportation (INDOT) permanently closed three intersections within unincorporated Johnson County, including the SR 37 and Fairview Road interchange. This closure altered local circulation patterns, reduced direct passerby traffic, and contributed to business relocations in the immediate area. In anticipation of I-69, Johnson County partnered with a planning consultant to develop the I-69 Corridor Plan, which was adopted in December 2018 as a supplement to the Johnson County Comprehensive Plan. The plan aimed to establish high-quality architectural and land-use standards for the I-69 gateway into the county, explicitly identifying certain vehicular-oriented commercial uses as undesirable for new development. When the county adopted the updated Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) in 2024, these plan recommendations were codified into the Corridor Overlay District (COD) regulations. The COD establishes elevated design and development standards for sites, structures, landscaping, signage, and site improvements within highly visible county corridors to: 7 Promote High-Quality Design: Encourage creative, innovative, and visually cohesive site and building development. Protect Property Values & Welfare: Preserve long-term property values and promote public health, safety, and welfare through consistent, coordinated development standards. Ensure Efficient & Coordinated Development: Establish high standards that optimize land use, permit flexible site design, and protect the functional integrity and visual character of major transportation corridors. Because the COD regulations explicitly prohibit automobile sales, service, and repair, the proposed operation requires Use Variance approval from the Board of Zoning Appeals. The Future Land Use Map within the I-69 Corridor Plan designates this immediate area for Residential development. However, staff believes this designation was an analytical oversight during the 2018 planning process, as this specific node south of Fairview Road contains existing, built-out commercial development that is not discussed or recommended for residential transition elsewhere in the document. Staff feels a Mixed-Use designation would have been more appropriate for this node. The overall narrative of the I-69 Corridor Plan explicitly seeks to maintain economic vitality and support the adaptive reuse of existing commercial properties impacted by INDOT access closures along secondary frontage networks. While general commercial reuse of this built-out site aligns with the plan's economic vitality goals, auto sales and repair specifically are restricted by the COD regulations to uphold the corridor’s elevated visual standards—hence the necessity of the requested Use Variance. While this report focuses primarily on the land use request, any future development of the vacant Lot 4 will be subject to the standard Site Plan Review process. Lot 4 must adhere to all UDO development standards. Staff notes that the preliminary layout shown on the submitted site plan will likely change once formal site development and drainage requirements are fully engineered. No Development Standard Variances are requested at this time, as the petitioner wishes to secure land use approval prior to committing to full site engineering. To address potential visual impacts on the corridor without requiring immediate development variances, Staff has drafted specific conditions of approval aimed at managing outdoor staging and display areas. STAFF RECOMMENDATION Should the Board move to approve this request, Staff recommends the inclusion of the following commitments/conditions: 1. Lot 4 Use Restriction: Lot 4 shall be utilized exclusively for product display and staging. 2. Surfacing Requirement: Any development or staging area on Lot 4 shall be constructed with a hard, durable surface. 3. The product display and staging area shall be subject to the same standards as a parking lot, especially Chapter 3 Section 3,c and Section B,5,b,c and Chapter 3 Section C,5,c. Staff would strongly suggest considering interior landscaping as well if the paved area is to be over 1.5 acres. 8 4. Fencing Standards: If fencing is installed on Lot 4, chain-link fencing (with or without barbed wire) is strictly prohibited. Fencing must consist of wrought iron or high-quality privacy fencing materials. 5. No Outdoor Storage of Repair/Parts: No outdoor storage of items awaiting repair, salvage parts, or loose materials shall be permitted on either parcel (Lot 3 or Lot 4). FINDINGS OF FACT: USE VARIANCE State Requirement: The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. The subject site includes an existing, vacant commercial building on Lot 3 originally developed in 1997. Granting a Use Variance to allow the sales, repair, and rental of trailers, truck beds, and golf carts within this existing structure returns a vacant property to productive commercial use. Furthermore, restricting Lot 4 strictly to a heavily conditioned, high-quality staging and display area (or leaving it undeveloped) prevents unmitigated commercial expansion, thereby safeguarding the visual environment, public safety, and general welfare of the corridor. State Requirement: The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will not be affected in a substantially adverse manner. Reoccupying the vacant building on Lot 3 eliminates a long-standing vacancy that risks becoming a visual blight along Western Boulevard following INDOT's access closures. Surrounding properties are established commercial lots of similar character. By revitalizing the existing structure, the variance stabilizes local property values. To protect adjacent parcels from potential visual degradation associated with expanding commercial operations, approval is tied to strict conditions that prohibit open storage of parts or items needing repair and ensure that any use of the vacant Lot 4 is strictly limited to screened display rather than intensive site development or heavy industrial staging. State Requirement: The need for the variance arises from some condition peculiar to the property involved. The property features a unique duality: a fully built-out commercial structure (Lot 3) that was rendered vacant and functionally isolated due to INDOT's closure of the Fairview Road/SR 37 intersection, paired with an adjacent undeveloped parcel (Lot 4) separated by a public road. The existing building was constructed under prior standards for vehicular commercial activity, making its footprint well-suited for adaptive indoor reuse. However, the 2024 Corridor Overlay District (COD) standards strictly prohibit these land uses. This structural layout—a purpose-built commercial building stranded by transportation network changes—creates a unique hardship that can be remedied by allowing indoor adaptive reuse without endorsing the unrestricted build-out of the adjacent undeveloped land. State Requirement: The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will constitute an unnecessary hardship if applied to the property for which a variance is sought. Strict enforcement of the Corridor Overlay District (COD) prohibition against vehicle sales and service would prevent the economic reuse of a purpose-built, 2.04-acre commercial site (Lot 3) that already possesses the necessary building footprint and pavement. Forcing this established building to remain vacant—particularly after state-initiated access closures reduced passerby traffic—imposes an unnecessary economic hardship. Allowing the requested use inside the existing structure relieves this hardship while preserving the Board's discretion to apply strict development standards or limitations on the undeveloped Lot 4 to prevent unnecessary visual appearance. 9 State Requirement: The approval does not interfere substantially with the Comprehensive Plan. The I-69 Corridor Plan explicitly encourages economic vitality and the adaptive reuse of existing commercial inventory impacted by I-69 access modifications along secondary frontage roads. While the plan seeks to prevent the uncontrolled proliferation of roadside vehicle lots along the corridor, permitting the adaptive reuse of the existing structure on Lot 3 directly fulfills the plan's economic revitalization goals. By capping the intensity of the use and enforcing strict design and buffering standards on any proposed staging on Lot 4, the approval honors both the plan's economic goals and its intent to elevate the visual gateway standards of Johnson County.. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This 2.56-acre site is zoned SR (Single-Family Residential) and is currently improved with a single-family dwelling and one accessory structure. The area surrounding this parcel consists of parcels of similar size, all used residentially. The properties directly to the west are located within the municipal limits of the town of Bargersville. VARIANCE REQUEST – DEVELOPMENT STANDARD The applicant is requesting a Variance of Development Standard to allow the construction of a 2,952-square-foot accessory structure on the subject property. The site currently contains two accessory structures: a 1,440-square-foot detached garage and a 96-square-foot shed. With the addition of the proposed 2,952-square-foot building, the total aggregate area of all three accessory structures would be 4,488 square feet. This exceeds the square footage of the primary dwelling, which is 2,912 square feet. The zoning ordinance stipulates that the total aggregate area of all accessory structures on a single lot shall not exceed 100% of the square footage of the primary dwelling (proposed at ~154%). Myers Representative County Council 1/1/2026 - 12/31/2026 Ron Bates Alternate Member - County Council 1/1/2026 - 12/31/2026 Greg Cantwell Surveyor - Office Held Office Term Shalee Bradley ANR County Extension Agent - Office Held Office Term Charles Canary Citizen Member appointed by County Commissioners 1/1/2023 - 12/31/2027 Douglas Gray Citizen Member appointed by County Commissioners 1/1/2024 - 12/31/2027 Steven Hickman Citizen Member appointed by County Commissioners 1/1/2023 - 12/31/2027 Robert Page Citizen Member appointed by County Commissioners 1/1/2024 - 12/31/2027 Stoney Vann Citizen Member appointed by County Commissioners 1/1/2025 - 12/31/2028 UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE – 2026 Amendment proposal The Department of Planning and Zoning has prepared a series of proposed text amendments to the Johnson County Uniﬁed Development Ordinance (UDO). Following the comprehensive adoption of the UDO in 2024, staff have identiﬁed several areas requiring technical cleanup, administrative clariﬁcation, and legislative updates. The proposed changes cover key operational areas including statutory protections for shooting ranges, deﬁned standards for event centers and group homes, clariﬁcation of accessory dwelling unit and structure sizes, and relief from suburban standards (such as sidewalks and individual lot landscaping) in rural and agricultural zoning districts.  Draft Redline Version of UDO Amendments as of 8-14-26  List of track changes to the UDO Below is the only amendment that was not voted on from the August meeting Group Home and Nursing Homes Rationale: Updates were made to the group home standards to align county zoning regulations better with ADA and federal fair housing guidelines, while resolving internal code inconsistencies across residential zoning districts. Deﬁnition & Scale: The UDO explicitly distinguishes a Group Home from larger institutional facilities, such as commercial nursing or convalescent centers. This distinction ensures group homes operate within a typical residential scale and character. State Compliance: Standards were updated to reference appropriate state licensing bodies—speciﬁcally the Division of Disability and Rehabilitative Services (DDRS) and the Division of Mental Health and Addiction (DMHA)—ensuring local oversight supports, rather than conﬂicts with, state licensing mandates. Permitted Districts & Occupancy Caps: Clariﬁed standards across residential and agricultural districts. Occupancy remains capped at eight (8) residents (excluding support staff) to maintain compatibility with single-family residential neighborhoods while ensuring compliance with federal Fair Housing Act protections for group living arrangements. Permitting & Review Process: Streamlined the review framework to clarify when a facility is permitted by right versus when it requires special approval, eliminating previous ambiguity surrounding unlisted uses or special exception requirements for state-licensed residential care homes. Requires a development plan to be submitted per Sec. 8.B.9, Development Plan Process, for the land use to be permitted. Amendment 2025-Z-1 105 b. Amphitheater stages and drive-in screens shall face away from the nearest residential uses (if any residential uses exist within 1,000 ft.) and any street of a classiﬁcation of collector or higher; c. For activities such as midget auto-track or a go-cart track, and if the use is in any way powered by an internal combustion engine, then such shall provide adequate muﬄers on all vehicles; and d. If the use is located within ﬁve hundred (500) feet from a residentially zoned property or residential use then the commercial amusement shall be prohibited from operating between 12:30 AM and 8:00 AM. 18. Contractor’s Shop. a. The only storage permitted shall be the storage necessary for the primary use to store operable equipment, materials, and associated items, which must be stored within an enclosed building or totally screened from view. This may include the storage of liquids, gels, and pastes (e.g., paints, sealers, etc.) provided that the use is stored only in enclosed buildings. b. The use shall not be used to dispose of inoperable machine waste or to rent storage space out to those not working regularly on the premises. 19. Correctional Institution. The use shall be located no closer than ﬁve hundred (500) feet from any residential district or use as measured along a straight line from the closest lot lines. 20. Crematorium. The use shall be in compliance with all federal, state, and local environmental regulations. 21. Farm Equipment and Repair. The use shall be located no closer than ﬁve hundred (500) feet from any residential district or use as measured along a straight line from the closest lot lines. 22. Group Home a. Group homes in the AG, AR, SR, and DR districts shall house a maximum of eight (8) unrelated individuals. Group homes in dwelling districts shall be designed to be residential in character and use similar architecture, design, materials and landscaping as adjacent and nearby Dwellings. b. 21. 22.23. Greenhouse / Nursery. All sales must be products created and/or produced on-site. Oﬀ- site shipments of products to the site are expressly prohibited. 23.24. Heavy Equipment Sales and Rentals. a. All equipment stored outside the principal business shall: 1) Be located on an asphalt or concrete surface; 112 proposed sand and gravel mining pit. The sampling and analysis plan shall contain speciﬁc information, including: 1) Site Background; 2) Sample Location Points; 3) Monitoring parameters (at a minimum, this should include regulated drinking water metals and organic and inorganic primary and secondary drinking water parameters regulated by IDEM under 327 IAC 8 and the Environmental Protection Agency for Public Water Supply Systems, and any other contaminants required by the Johnson County Planning Department); 4) Analytical methods (analysis shall be by a laboratory certiﬁed to perform the analysis utilizing the most recent test methods and regulatory limits); 5) Detection limits; 6) Sampling personnel; 7) Decontamination procedures; 8) Water level measurement and purging; 9) Sample collection procedures and preservation; 10) Quality control; 11) Sample management; 12) Chain of custody; and 13) Sampling event reporting e. Reclamation Plan. A reclamation plan which outlines the scope, scale, and cost of associated remediation to enable the aﬀected land use to be reused. 39. Nursing Home a. Nursing homes shall be licensed by the Indiana State Department of Health and obtain, comply with, and maintain any required license from the Johnson County Health Department. b. Nursing homes in dwelling districts shall be designed to be residential in character. e.c.Nursing homes shall be designed with appropriate access and maneuverability for emergency vehicles 38.40. Oﬃce, General. In the PR District, the use is limited to oﬃce space secondary to another land use that is allowed within the PR District. 39.41. Place of Public Assembly, Indoor. A minimum lot size of two (2) acres shall be required for the use to locate on the property. 40.42. Recreational Vehicle Park and Campground. 239 GROUP HOME: A residential structure or facility where six (6) or more unrelated persons who are in need of care, support or supervision can live together, such as children or those who are elderly, disabled or mentally ill. Group Homes housing persons with developmental disabilities shall obtain, comply with, and maintain a license from the Indiana Division of Disability and Rehabilitative Services. Group Homes housing those living with psychiatric disorders or addictions shall obtain, comply with, and maintain a license from the Indiana Division of Mental Health and Addictions . A non-proﬁt or for- proﬁt group home regulated under IC 31-27 for the sheltered care of persons with special needs, which, in addition to providing food and shelter, may also provide some combination of personal care, social or counseling services, and transportation. GUARANTEE: Cash, bonds, or similar ﬁnancial instruments deposited with the County to ensure that required improvements will be constructed or installed. HEAVY EQUIPMENT SALES AND RENTALS: A business engaged in the rental or sales of powered heavy mechanical equipment. HEIGHT: The distance from the ground where the structure stands to the highest point of the structure. HOME BUSINESS: A lawful activity conducted for ﬁnancial gain, where such use does not include the sale of goods to customers on the premises or opening of the home to the public for the sale of goods or services without an invitation or appointment. The use diﬀers from a home occupation in that mechanical equipment related to the use may be stored outside of the building provided that proper screening is provided. Minimal traﬃc shall be required to occur on the property so that there is minimal disruption to the neighborhood. HOME OCCUPATION: An occupation, profession, domestic craft, or economic enterprise which is customarily conducted in a residential dwelling. The use diﬀers from a home business in that there shall be no outside indication that a business is operated on the site. HOMEOWNER’S ASSOCIATION: A formally constituted non-proﬁt association or corporation made up of the property owners and/or residents of a deﬁned area; who collectively may take permanent responsibility for costs and upkeep of commonly owned or designated community property. HOSPITAL / REHABILITATIVE CARE: An institution providing primary health services and medical or surgical care to persons, primarily inpatients, suﬀering from illness, disease, injury, disability, and other physical or mental conditions and including, as an integral part of the institution, related facilities, such as laboratories, outpatient facilities, training facilities, medical oﬃces, and staﬀ residences. This includes a clinic, hospital, or sanitarium, except a criminal, mental, or animal hospital; and nursing or convalescent home. HOTEL: A commercial building in which lodging is provided and oﬀered to the public for compensation. Planning Commission
The Planning Commission meets to review and make findings on development plans for subdivisions, commercial structures, industrial structures and planned unit developments within the Commission's jurisdiction. They also review and revise the zoning ordinance , subdivision regulations, and other land use regulations to keep them up-to-date.
The meeting dates can be found below in Relevant Documents. You may also watch the meetings live on our YouTube Channel .

items.title: Board of Zoning Appeals | Town of Prince’s Lakes
items.text:
Board of Zoning Appeals
The Board of Zoning Appeals meets to approve or deny variances from the development standards (such as height, bulk or area) of the zoning ordinance. They approve or deny all special exceptions, special uses, contingent uses and conditional uses pertaining to cases or the particular situations specified in the zoning ordinance.
The Board of Zoning Appeals shall hear and determine appeals from and review:
(1) any order, requirement, decision, or determination made by an administrative official, hearing officer, or staff member under the zoning ordinance;
(2) any order, requirement, decision, or determination made by an administrative board or other body except a plan commission in relation to the enforcement of the zoning ordinance; or
(3) any order, requirement, decision, or determination made by an administrative board or other body except a plan commission in relation to the enforcement of an ordinance adopted under the chapter requiring the procurement of an improvement location or occupancy permit.
Applications and the meeting and filing dates can be found in the forms below.

items.title: Town Council | Town of Prince’s Lakes
items.text:
Town Council
The Town of Prince's Lakes Council acts as the legislative branch of our government, as well as its policy-making body. The Council looks to the Town's goals, major projects and infrastructure improvements ranging from community growth to land use to finances and strategic planning. The Council's goal is to do the very best to represent their constituents after they've seen to the needs of the Town as a whole.
Town Council meets the 3rd Monday of every month at 6:00 pm at Town Hall.

Document Center Board & Commission Openings
Board & Commission Openings
The Town of Edinburgh has several openings on various 2027 boards and commissions starting October 5, 2026.
· Planning Commission- one board member for a 4-year term. Qualified applicants must live within Town limits and be an elected official or an employee of the Town of Edinburgh.
· Board of Metropolitan Police Commissioners- one board member for a 3-year term. Qualified applicants live within Town limits.
· Joint Planning Commission- 2 board members for a 3-year term. Qualified applicants must live within Town limits.
· Edinburgh Redevelopment Commission- 6 board members for a 1-year term. Qualified applicants must live within Town limits.
· Economic Development Board- 2 board members; 1 board member for a 1-year term and 1 board member for a 2-year term. Qualified applicants must live within Town limits.
Applications are available on the Town website by clicking here or Town Hall located at 107 S Holland Street.
Completed applications should be mailed to PO Box 65, Edinburgh, IN 46124, dropped off at the Town Hall located at 107 S Holland Street, or emailed to townhall@edinburgh.in.us by November 6, 2026.

The Trafalgar Local Board of Finance is responsible for overseeing the financial management and investment practices of the Town of Trafalgar. Fiscal Accountability Promotes transparency and long-term financial stability through responsible stewardship of public resources.

The Trafalgar Park Board is appointed by the Town Council and plays a vital role in shaping the community’s parks and recreational spaces. The Board consists of four members who must be residents of the Town and are selected based on their interest in and knowledge of parks and recreation. No more than two members may be affiliated with the same political party unless the Town Council grants a waiver, as allowed under IND. CODE § 36-10-3-4.1 . items.title: Town of Whiteland: Board of Zoning Appeals
items.text:
The Whiteland Advisory Board of Zoning Appeals (“BZA”) works to ensure that zoning regulations are fairly applied across varying properties in town. Essentially, the BZA serves as a board to hear appeals that specific zoning regulations should be applied differently to a particular property due to certain conditions of the site or the proposed use. The administrative appeal is an appeal of a decision made by town staff regarding the zoning code. The BZA does not enforce the zoning code, but they can adjust the regulations for a property to suit its specific site conditions that would otherwise be in violation of the zoning code. The responsibilities of the BZA is as follows:
Indiana Code provides that the BZA has the following specific authorities:
Granting of variances Developmental standards variances Variances of use
Developmental standards variances
Variances of use
Granting of special exceptions (also known as conditional uses)
Appeals from administrative decisions
Members
Two members of the BZA are selected from the Plan Commission, two are appointed by the Town Council President, and one is appointed by the Town Council. By state code, members cannot hold any other elected or appointed position (except the two Plan Commission members).

items.title: Directions/Parking/Drop-Off/Pick-Up - Center Grove High School
items.text:
Directions/Parking/Drop-Off/Pick-Up
CGHS Pick-Up/Drop Off
Directions to CGHS
CGHS Daily/Event Parking
Traffic routes around the Center Grove High School have been updated for the 2025-26 school year. These changes are designed to improve safety, reduce traffic back-up on Morgantown Road, and improve traffic flow - based on feedback we received last year.
STUDENT DROP-OFF AND PICK-UP Parents dropping off and picking up students from Center Grove High School should enter the high school campus by turning off of Morgantown Road onto Pennington Drive. Traffic on Pennington will continue through the peanut-shaped roundabout to east of the Tennis Complex and into the lot between the Innovation Center and Baseball Field. (See map below.) Parents will then continue north through the lot to the exit and turn left (south) back onto Trojan Lane. They will travel west, past the Tennis Complex, and turn right (north) onto Victory Lane to enter the drop-off/pick-up line. Drop-off is at Door #9, the same as prior years. This is the only location where students should be dropped off at school. Parents will then exit the campus by following Victory Lane to the roundabout at the intersection with Trojan Lane and continue north to Stones Crossing Road.
STUDENT PARKING FOOTBALL STUDENT LOT: Students may enter the parking lot east of the football stadium from Morgantown Road. They should take Pennington Road straight through the peanut-shaped roundabout, and curve around to Trojan Lane. There is no access from the north on Trojan Lane before school to this lot. This is not a change from prior years, however, students will be permitted to exit via Morgantown or Stones Crossing after school this year. Please note that this traffic will merge at the roundabout with parent pick-up traffic and students exiting the north lots.
NORTH STUDENT LOTS: Students may enter the north student lots from Stones Crossing Road. They should turn onto Trojan Lane and turn right into the student lot. (This is not a change from prior years.) GATE RESTRICTIONS Gates will be down on Pennington Road at the peanut to restrict traffic from turning left onto Victory Lane and on Trojan Lane just south of the roundabout from 7:30-8:05 AM when school is in session. The Pennington Road gate will also be down from 2:15-3:15 PM.
DURING SCHOOL PICK-UP AND DROP-OFF During the school day, students who are dropped off and picked up for appointments or late arrivals should use Door #9 (Hall of Excellence), where they will check in with staff at the security vestibule. After 1:30 PM, students may be picked up for appointments from Door #1should use the front administrative entrance (Door #1) at the flagpole/electronic sign off of Morgantown Road. Parents who need to come into the building should also use Door #1.
AFTER SCHOOL ACTIVITY DROP-OFF AND PICK-UP Parents dropping off and picking up students of any age for activities at Center Grove High School must follow the traffic markings around the high school.

JACK RUSSELL President, CGCSC Board of School Trustees
Jack Russell is a long-time resident of the Center Grove community. He graduated from Center Grove High School in 1974. He is a graduate of Purdue University where he studied Elementary Education. After Purdue, Mr. Russell attended Butler University to study dance and acting.
Russell spent time traveling the country after graduation doing live shows at theme parks and dinner theaters. During that time, he would also substitute teach in the local school system. After a few years working as general manager in his family’s real estate and development business, Russell returned to the world of education to teach full-time. He also spent time substitute teaching while raising his son, Austin, whom he adopted from Paraguay. Austin is a 2013 Center Grove graduate.
Russell has been an active member of the Center Grove Education Foundation. He is also involved with the Center Grove Alumni and Friends group. Russell was elected to the Center Grove Board of School Trustees in 2010 and has served in various leadership positions, including as president in 2013.
SCOTT ALEXANDER Vice President, CGCSC Board of School Trustees
Scott Alexander is a 1991 graduate of Center Grove High School and a lifelong Center Grove resident. He received his bachelor’s degree from Purdue University in 1995. Mr. Alexander is the Vice President, of Sales and Strategic Partnerships for InTempo Software.
Alexander joined Center Grove’s Board of School Trustees in 2010. Prior to that he was a four-year member of the Center Grove Education Foundation.
Alexander's Information Technology background spans over the past 18 years with experience in various leadership roles. He has spent a large portion of his career in the pharmaceutical and healthcare industries with some experience in consulting as well. Alexander brings vast experience in leading teams and businesses of varying sizes through information technology, operations, and logistics.
Alexander and his wife, Dana, have two sons who are graduates of Center Grove High School. In his spare time, he enjoys playing golf.
JANE DUNIGAN-SMITH Secretary, CGCSC Board of School Trustees
Jane Dunigan-Smith has lived in the Center Grove community for more than 22 years. She is the Senior Vice President and Chief Strategy Officer at BioCrossroads. Dunigan-Smith has a master’s degree in business administration, marketing and strategy and a bachelor’s degree in accounting and finance from the Kelley School of Business at Indiana University, Bloomington.
Dunigan-Smith has served on the Board of the Center Grove Education Foundation and is a graduate of the Center Grove Ambassadors program. She and her husband, Rodney, have two sons, one graduate of Center Grove High School (CGHS) and a senior at CGHS.
