items.title: Meeting of the Greenwood Common Council Minutes 9.21.26
items.text: Meeting of the Greenwood Common Council MINUTES Date: September 21, 2026 Time: 7:00 pm Place: Council Chamber 300 S Madison Ave Greenwood, Indiana I. Call Meeting to Order A. Pledge of Allegiance B. Prayer: David Denny - lay leader at Victory Baptist Church C. Roll Call: Council Members Present: Mike Campbell ("Mr. Campbell"), Linda Gibson ("Ms. Gibson"), Ezra Hill ("Mr. Hill"), David Hopper ("Mr. Hopper"), Erin Kasch ("Ms. Kasch"), David Lekse, ("Mr. Lekse"), Teri Manship, ("Ms. Manship"), Steve Moan ("Mr. Moan") Darin Hoggatt ("Mr. Hoggatt") City Officials: Mark Myers (“Mayor Myers”) Jeannine Myers ("Ms. Myers") Clerk, Greg Wright ("Mr. Wright") Controller, Sam Hodson (“Mr. Hodson”) Corporation Council, James Ison ("Chief Ison") Police Chief, Jayme Washel (“Chief Washel”) Fire Chief, Drew Foster (“Judge Foster”) City Judge, and Department Heads. Council President Campbell reminded attendees that respectful participation is expected and that disruptions are not permitted. This will be read before each meeting: Before we begin, I want to remind everyone that respectful participation is expected. We welcome public input at the appropriate times, but there will be no yelling or interruptions that prevent the meeting from moving forward. Anyone who disrupts the meeting will be asked to leave and may be escorted out. II. Approval of Minutes A. Minutes from the regular meeting September 9 ,2026 Motion to approve regular meeting minutes from September 9, 2026 by Kasch, seconded by Hill Votes: Ayes – Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hopper Kasch Abstain: Lekse, Manship, Moan, Hoggatt Motion Passes: 5-0 with 4 abstentions III. Reports A. Corporation Counsel B. Controller C. Committee & Board Report IV. Public Comments This timeslot is for residents who would like to address the Council about matters on the agenda. All materials presented at a public meeting are considered part of the official record; please provide a copy to the Clerk. Individuals- 5-minute time limit; Groups- 20-minute time limit Deann Lautenbach, 2255 S. Franklin Rd, Greenwood, IN 46143 I live at the corner of Franklin and Clark Road in Greenwood. I'm an aggravated and affected neighbor due to living in the middle of the unfinished corridor between 65 and 74, which will be feeding an enormous amount of traffic to the destination travel center, being one of the largest gas stations in the entire state of Indiana. I am here tonight to establish a formal legally binding administrative record against docket PC 2026-035. To fully preserve my right to file a judicial review in the Johnson County courts. I request that this Council table this back to the Planning Commission or deny this petition because it creates a severe procedural violation, breaks local ordinances, and creates a textbook, arbitrary, capricious action. Indiana open door law. Under Indiana Code Section 5.14 1.55, public agencies are required to give public notice of their meetings, including posting an agenda if one is utilized at least 48 hours in advance, excluding weekends and legal holidays, dropping a major, unvetted, supplemental traffic study on a Friday afternoon for a Monday vote, actively circumvents the transparency mandated by the state sunshine law. Greenwood Planning Division staff report ruled: after an examination of information in the public record and findings from additional research, staff shall publish a technical review committee report that provides an analysis of the petition request. Such reports shall be published along with an agenda approximately five days prior to the meeting. By failing to give a five-day buffer, the city directly broke its own local guidelines. Indiana Code Section 3674607. This statute dictates that any zoning ordinance or planned unit development text amendment must follow a strict process between the Planning Commission and the Legislative Council. Under Indiana Land Use law, if a developer introduces significant technical updates or modifications after the Planning Commission has already voted, the Common Council is legally required to remand the proposal back to the Planning Commission. This ensures that the public hearing body can officially investigate, review, and certify the new data before a final vote takes place. Indiana Code Section 3674604. This statute mandates that a major zoning ordinance or text amendment cannot be legally enacted without a formal, legally advertised public hearing because the brand-new September 15th traffic memo reveals a severe level of service F gridlock. Failures right at our local school entrances, avenues, and because this data was hidden from the public portal until Friday afternoon, the community has never been granted a valid public hearing on the actual material facts of this case. I gave you guys all exhibits. Exhibit A: The build, this is from the traffic study, build 2037 capacity reports from Section F, all the traffic study. This document proves that the intersection of Emerson Avenue and Worthsville Road will suffer complete gridlock during peak morning school hours. The northbound approach drops to a level of service grade F, forcing parents, teachers, and school buses to face a catastrophic average delay of 275.26 seconds, which is over four and a half minutes. Of forced idling per vehicle. This extensive line of cars will stack directly backward during the morning peak hour, clogging the entrance avenues of Clark Pleasant Middle School and creating a dangerous hazard gridlock where student commuters are trapped in stationary traffic. Exhibit B: The existing 2026 plus site capacity reports from Section D of the study. This proves that the infrastructure will fail on day one. The very moment this site opens, page two reveals that the southbound approach directly exiting the Grassy Creek Elementary School access road completely breaks down into an immediate level of service F, forcing parents and school buses to idle for 74.9 seconds, over a minute each just to exit the school gates. Furthermore, page four exposed a catastrophic four-way systematic breakdown at county roads. 200 East and Worthsville Road, where the northbound and southbound approaches simultaneously fail at level service F, blocking up primary school access road with immediate delays up to three and a half minutes. Exhibit C, and I have more, but I can't. proving the developers actively breaking our local laws to circumvent safety protections, unifying development ordinances section 100107 with the illegal spot zoning. That's going on. I need to put that in the record so I can file a judicial review. Furthermore, your master plan used on table 17 completely bans travel plazas. That is illegal spot zoning. The developer is also proposing to remove an active timed travel traffic signal along the corridor and replace it with a roundabout element, eliminating the only mechanical guarantee that stops commercial traffic to let parents in school buses. Thank you. Kim Crawford, 166 Caplinger Place, Greenwood, In 46143 I am also the school board president for the Clark Pleasant Community School Corporation. Council President, Council Members, and City staff, thank you for the opportunity to speak this evening. I am here on behalf of the Clark Pleasant Community School Corporations and the families we serve. We appreciate the city and Buc-ee’s for conducting an initial traffic study and for sharing the updated remote this last week. We're not opposed to the development. However, we do have significant concerns about what the updated study demonstrates and the limited scope of the proposed mitigations. Our responsibility is to ensure that any changes along Worthsville Road support safe, reliable operations for our students, families, and our bus drivers. The updated Buc-ee’s traffic study provides new data on projected traffic volumes and interception performance during school drop-off and pickup windows. Although the city concludes that the site “does not result in significant additional traffic impacts during school- related peak periods,” several findings, including our own observations, indicate meaningful concerns for school operations and student safety. First, school peak traffic is already operating at a near rush-hour intensity. PM drop-off volumes are only about 50 vehicles lower than evening rush-hour peak. Because these peaks do not overlap, Buc-ee’s traffic represents additional load, not shared load. Second, the multiple intersections show significant delay growth between current conditions and 2037 projections. Worthsville and Emerson (northbound) shows substantial increases in delay in the report. Worthsville and Southlake (southbound) already experiences significant drop-off delays and it's projected to nearly double. Worthsville Road and County Road 200 shows delays exceeding 120 seconds or two minutes today- both AM southbound and PM northbound with worsening delays projected. These are the same intersections that our buses and our student drivers and our families use in order to get to the middle school and the two elementary schools there. Third Buc-ee’s is projected to add 1,045 trips during the morning drop-off and 1,380 trips during afternoon pickup. The study attempts to differentiate where these trips go afterwards, but the impact occurs the moment we enter the roadway, Worthsville Road. During compressed school windows, any added volume destabilizes flow. Fourth, only one mitigation has been proposed, re-striving at the southbound approach at Worthsville Road and Ray Crowe Way. And this is the entrance to the middle school. No other improvements have been recommended for intersections already showing severe delays. If striking Ray Crowe Way was the solution, we would have thought about it and would have done it before now. Finally, despite these findings, the study concludes that Buc-ee's does not result in significant additional traffic impacts during school-related periods. This conclusion does not align with the data that was presented or with school-specific traffic behavior. Because of these concerns, the district respectfully requests a formal commitment from the city and Buc-ee’s. If Buc-ee's operations create significant negative impact on our instructional day, bus routing our on-time performance, or parent pickup and drop-off operations, we just asking that the city and Buc-ee’s re-engage with us collaboratively to identify and implement mitigation strategies, including additional studies or infrastructure improvements. There's very little we can do on our own without more help. Our focus is simple: to ensure that the daily experience of our students, families, and staff remains safe and predictable as this progress progresses. We value our partnership with the city and Buc- ee’s and we want to continue to work together constructively. Thank you for your time and attention. Tim Edsell, Clark-Pleasant School Superintendent Appreciate your leadership. Again, I appreciate a couple of you who met with me individually. Appreciate you listening. I appreciate Scott Ratcliffe, who is one of the senior engineers for Buc-ee’s, for producing the revised traffic study. To me and to us as a school corporation last week. I appreciate them willing to redo the traffic study that last week of August. President Crawford just said a lot of similar points. I'll reiterate a few of them, but not to be repetitive and for the sake of brevity. I do want to emphasize some of those key areas that are of concern to us with the traffic flow That would be Worthsville & Emerson, Worthsville & South Lake Avenue, and Worthsville & County Rd 200 The one suggestion to obviously reach strike the left and turn lanes that's on our property right by middle school entrance. Appreciate that. We could do that. Signage, we could do that. My final request would be: as Buc-ee’s is built, I would love to see improved and stronger communication from all entities because, as it's built and even as it opens up, whatever that timeframe is, and the impact that it will have on our school day is so significant. I would love to work together with, again, all entities because it's important that obviously we conduct school. I've made our Department of Education aware of this. And so, the goal is for us, to work with you, not to be against you, but to make sure that we have school every single day within the required hours that were allotted. Thank you for your time. Mitch Hunter. I live at 3114 East 700 North in Whiteland, Indiana, 46184. Updating the comprehensive plan involves not only community input, hiring the third-party companies of HWC Engineering and Stantec. The project siphoned $200,000 from the city budget. The goal was for the final project to be “the blueprint for the future.” The land in question tonight falls in a major part of that blueprint, one the city deemed worthy of developing a specific vision for how the area will be used and what it would look like in the years to come (Greenwood Crossing). The plan says it is critical that this area holds a strong set of development criteria to ensure new development allows the city to grow its tax base, of course, but also to protect adjacent rural lifestyles. The new plan acknowledges Greenwood residents expressed their concern throughout the process about industrial development continuing south past Worthsville Road. Additionally, the HWC Steering Committee held a meeting specifically addressing the future land use of this area. The very first bullet point meeting states: “Areas surrounding the I-65 and Worthsville Road interchange should remain largely residential with limited commercial uses that serve the surrounding neighborhoods and not those traveling along the highway.” There are two major issues regarding this land and its proposed use. First, the community repeatedly expressed its concern about industrial and warehouse development in the area. Similar projects in the area have not come to fruition because the city listened to the residents and honored their promise to prevent industrial developments. But it's important to note that the problem with proposed industrial developments in the past was not with the business of logistics itself. Rather, it is what those businesses bring to the land: massive structures, invasive lighting, and daunting amounts of traffic. Though not in the business of logistics, a Buc-ee’s brings all of those things front and center, industrial or not. Even though they themselves clearly thought that their operations warranted industrial classifications when they originally brought this before the APC. The spirit of no warehouses and no industrial was to guard against these types of developments. Secondly, allowing this development or any like it will destroy the vision for Greenwood Crossing. The plan calls for a development that is harmonious with residential development on adjacent properties. However, a 120-pump gas station is a poisoned pill. It spoils the land around it. Here is a visual of 37 Buc-ee’s across the United States. I emailed this to each of you earlier. Thank you for those that responded, confirming that you received it. What it shows here is there's a radius of 2,500 feet from the proposed site. The distance that in our plan is supposed to be residential. And when you look at that, you will see that there is no new housing development in any of those 37. Maybe some was existing, but nothing new. All that comes afterwards is warehouses and other large-scale development buildings. Every Buc-ee’s dead zone is a far cry from what Greenwood Crossing is supposed to be, from what we spent $200,000 to plan, and from what this Council promised was in our future. Thank You Mike Venatta, 1085 S Nay Rd, Greenwood, retired. We built our house 25 years ago on Nay Road. And I see several things with Buc-ee’s, and I'm not anti-Buc-ee’s. I'm anti-the location of this Buc-ee’s in Greenwood at this particular location. One, it really doesn't bring hundreds of pre-paying jobs. If you look at it close it brings jobs that are almost identical to the warehouse jobs that we've got now in Greenwood. Of the 200 jobs there, five of them would have enough money to buy a medium-sized house in the city of Greenwood. Again, I'm not putting down the job thing. What is important is, I think, what the last gentleman said quite a bit, and the confusion that's out there, if you look, I just got this letter today from INDOT, and it was something I've been requesting. And thank goodness they shared the traffic info with these other people first. But I'm going to read you, if you would, and if you trust an old guy that's 75 years old. What you see on the internet when you pull this up. Last Friday, I did an AI overview request on the I-65 of Worthsville Road Interchange looking for this new study. Here's what I got: the I-65 of Worthsville Road Interchange in Greenwood, Indiana, can handle roughly 23,000 vehicles per day, but traffic data shows it is already pushing its design limits. Daily capacity recent traffic impact studies and local projections highlight that the current volume of 23,000 vehicles daily already causes the interchange to approach or fail standard design levels during peak hours. The diverging diamond interchange, which Mayor Myers bragged about and should have years ago, about taking the load off the south side, keeping traffic moving smoothly. And remember, we have neighbors too, Whiteland, New Whiteland, that are building up like crazy. But it says “this interchange is highly effective at moving traffic efficiently without requiring left turns. However, area growth from local schools, (God bless them), and residential developments has heavily burdened its capacity. Buc-ee’s impact: Travel projections show that adding an estimated 15,000 new daily trips on top of the existing 23,000 vehicles would cause the intersection flow to fail completely. And here's something I want to ask you guys to consider deeply. I'm old, I can watch YouTube, and I love watching that. Here's Indiana, here's the growing counties, here's the growing cities. Greenwood's been on there, and one of the major advantages of Greenwood is being close to Indianapolis. And not having congestion to get there. They have said repeatedly with Fishers and Carmel, I-69 is a mess every morning. So, I want you to consider this, if you would, please. Of the estimated daily vehicles, and this is the breakdown, I guess, the way that Buc-ee’s does it: pass by intercept: 10,500 to 12,000 is existing highway traffic pulling off and returning to I-65. No new cars added. Great. The next one: primary new trips, brand new trips generated to local roads explicitly to visit Buc-ee’s. Think Indianapolis, think Franklin, think Shelbyville, think Bloomington, think everywhere. That the total estimated daily vehicles, and this is non-interstate, is 3000-4500. I'm not a traffic analyst by any means. I'm college educated. I do have 40 years of corporate experience, but don't tell me that Greenwood isn't facing congestion now on holidays and weekends. And how do you explain adding up to 4,500 more cars every day from local roads? It's not going to just affect us on the south side, it's going to affect all of Greenwood. And just please consider that. And plus, I guess to sum up, there's 1,500 homes or residents that are going to be affected, probably lose five to ten percent of their value. Mine's one of them. But that's just me personally. But everyone in Greenwood is going to be affected by the congestion and the other things. So please consider that, thank you for your time. Carmen Manson, 121 South Meridian Street, Greenwood, IN. I am for Buc-ee’s, I have been to 3 states, 4 Buc-ee’s and have never had a problem getting in or out. I've been to one as an open, never had a problem getting in or out. I love Buc-ee’s. I love the food. I love the people. I love the merchandise. I think it would be good for Greenwood. As the back of my shirt says, life is better at Buc-ee’s. I would love to see that sign that says 240 miles to Buc-ee’s to say Greenwood, to Buc-ee’s, to Worthsville Avenue, your next Buc-ee’s. So please vote yes. We want Buc-ee’s. And that's hundreds of people on Facebook next door, Greenwood Chatter, Center Grove Chatter, who have tied in and said, bring it. So, bring it. That takes care of the 20 minutes on Ordinance 26-24. Anyone else here that would like to speak to the council concerning another item that is on tonight’s agenda? If so, please step to the podium and state your name and address. Seeing none and moving on V. Ordinances and Resolutions A. Notice of Intent to Consider Ordinance No. 26-24 An Ordinance to amend the official zoning map adopted by reference and unified development Ordinance number 20-29. Proposed rezoning of approximately 80.15 acres located on the southeast corner of Interstate 65 & Worthsville Road. (Sponsors: Campbell, Gibson, Hopper, Lexi, and Manship) Is there a petitioner here? Good evening, Mr. President, members of the Common Council. My name is Bryan Tuohy. My address is 9294 North Meridian Street, and I'm here representing the petitioner, which is a company called CSMS Management LLC, which is an affiliate of Buc-ee's LLC. Here with me tonight is Scott Ratcliff, the Director of Engineering for Buc-ee’s, Angela Jarvik who's with Buc-ee’s Real Estate Department, Sammy Bijonowski, who's a traffic engineer with Kimley-Horn, and also Chad Mayes, the lead engineer for Kimley-Horn on this development. Thank you for hearing our case. May I make a presentation to the Council? Thank you, sir. So members of the Council, this site is an 80-acre site, as you've heard from some folks that spoke in here tonight. It's at the southeast corner of Worthsville Road and I-65. This first exhibit here shows that the site, there's next to no residential development around that site. To the north of it is a farm store and then a significantly sized, successful industrial park. On the west side of the site is Interstate 65. On the north side of the site is Worthsville Road. On the east side of the site is Collins Rd and County Road 250 East. That makes this site in the corner of this interstate a very attractive site for commercial development because it's bordered by three sides by three roads. When the Council is looking into rezoning one of the elements to look at is what does the comprehensive plan call for in the development of a particular site? And this slide here is from the Greenwood Comprehensive Plan future land use map. It actually has two classifications on this site. It calls it Greenwood Crossing and it calls for regional destination commercial land use. Let's look at what that means in your comprehensive plan. Regional destination commercial land use in your comprehensive plan says that this classification is designed to accommodate a range of potential entertainment, recreation, hospitality, and retail activities. There's no mention of residential activities in that opening paragraph describing regional destination commercial. That also goes on to say that those activities are generally in close proximity to Interstate 65. The site is right next to Interstate 65. It goes further on to say the defining characteristics of these uses is that customers will plan a special trip, there and value the overall experience. I think Buc-ee's meets a lot of those elements. So, you look down at the use table, it says the primary uses are retail, restaurant, recreation, entertainment, office, medical office, personal service, hotel, assisted living, event, venue center. Those are the kinds of uses you'd expect to develop around this Buc-ee’s and the kinds of uses that are allowed under this proposed planned unit of development. One thing that you also need to look at in the Comprehensive Plan that calls this Greenwood Crossing Conceptual Plan, it has some design principles. One of those design principles, the first one, is to develop a walkable mixed-use activity center serving as an anchor for new investment south of Worthsville. This is certainly new investment just south of Worthsville with a mix of commercial, hospitality, and office flex uses that capitalize on the interstate visibility. This site is right next to the interstate and access and have a potential to diversify the city's employment base, attract visitors, and fill the daily needs of nearby residents. We'll talk about that in a minute. But another element in that is city investment. It says the development should create a return on significant city investments in the area, including the sanitary sewer lift station, the sports park, extension of multi-use trails, and the fire station 95. This will represent a very significant investment. The zoning, underlying zoning, under the planet development zoning, is CL, commercial large zoning. And the plan commission has looked at this and also looked at the plat. The first thing to happen w

items.text: Meeting of the Greenwood Common Council ROLL CALL Date: October 5. 2026 Time: 7:00 pm Place: Council Chamber 300 S Madison Ave Greenwood, Indiana I. Call Meeting to Order A. Pledge of Allegiance B. Prayer: Gary Ryder, a long-time Greenwood resident and Air Traffic Controller C. Roll Call: Council Members Present: Mike Campbell ("Mr. Campbell"), Linda Gibson ("Ms. Gibson"), Ezra Hill ("Mr. Hill"), David Hopper ("Mr. Hopper"), Erin Kasch ("Ms. Kasch"), Teri Manship, ("Ms. Manship"), Steve Moan ("Mr. Moan") Darin Hoggatt ("Mr. Hoggatt") Absent: David Lekse, ("Mr. Lekse") City Officials: Mark Myers (“Mayor Myers”) Jeannine Myers ("Ms. Myers") Clerk, Greg Wright ("Mr. Wright") Controller, Sam Hodson (“Mr. Hodson”) Corporation Council, James Ison ("Chief Ison") Police Chief, Jayme Washel (“Chief Washel”) Fire Chief, and Department Heads. Council President Campbell reminded attendees that respectful participation is expected and that disruptions are not permitted. This will be read before each meeting: Before we begin, I want to remind everyone that respectful participation is expected. We welcome public input but there will be no yelling or interruptions that prevent the meeting from moving forward. Anyone who disrupts the meeting will be asked to leave and may be escorted out. II. Approval of Minutes A. Minutes from the regular meeting September 21,2026 Motion to postpone approval of minutes from September 9, 2026 by Moan, seconded by Manship. Votes: All Ayes B. Life Saving Award III. Reports A. Corporation Counsel B. Controller C. Committee & Board Report Greenwood Growth Speaker Series: TOPIC: What, Why, and Demand for Missing Middle Housing. Speaker(s): Chris Pryor, Chief Advocacy Officer, Brad Coffing, Director of Housing Insights IV. Public Comments This timeslot is for residents who would like to address the Council about matters on the agenda. All materials presented at a public meeting are considered part of the official record; please provide a copy to the Clerk. Individuals- 5-minute time limit; Groups- 20-minute time limit V. Ordinances and Resolutions A. Notice of Intent to Consider ORDINANCE NO. 26-36 AN ORDINANCE TO AMEND THE OFFICIAL ZONING MAP ADOPTED BY REFERENCE IN UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE NO. 20-29 (PROPOSED REZONING OF APPROXIMATELY 48.21 ACRES OF LAND COMMONLY KNOWN AS 903 W. STONES CROSSING ROAD) (Sponsored by Lekse) Motion to amend Ord. No. 26-36 motion to remove the word “additional” from item #5 and add no vinyl by Hopper seconded by Hoggatt Votes: Ayes - Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Hoggatt Votes: Nay-Moan Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-36 as amended by Hopper, seconded by Gibson Votes: Ayes - Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell Motion passes: 8-0 B. First Reading ORDINANCE NO. 26-30 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE COMMON COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-30 by Gibson, seconded by Kasch Votes: Ayes – Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson Motion passes: 8-0 ORDINANCE NO. 26-31 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE MAYOR OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-31 by Hoggatt, seconded by Manship Votes: Ayes – Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson, Hill Motion passes: 8-0 ORDINANCE NO. 26-32 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE CLERK OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-32 by Kasch, seconded by Moan Votes: Ayes -Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt Motion passes: 8-0 ORDINANCE NO. 26-33 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE CITY JUDGE OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027(Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-33 by Hopper, seconded by Moan Votes: Ayes - Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt, Kasch Motion passes: 8-0 ORDINANCE NO. 26-34 AN ORDINANCE FIXING SALARIES OF APPOINTED OFFICERS AND EMPLOYEES OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA AND CITY UTILITIES FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-34 by Hopper, seconded by Moan Votes: Ayes - Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch Motion passes: 8-0 ORDINANCE NO. 26-35 AN ORDINANCE FOR APPROPRIATIONS AND TAX RATES FOR THE 2027 BUDGET YEAR (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) Public Hearing scheduled for October 5, 2026 Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-35 by Hoggatt, seconded by Gibson Votes: Ayes - Moan, Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship Motion passes: 8-0 RESOLUTION NO. 26-09 A RESOLUTION DECLARING CERTAIN REAL PROPERTY IMPROVEMENTS FOR TAX ABATEMENT (Exeter Southtech Land, LLC- EQT Southtech Building 1) (Sponsored by Gibson) Motion to pass Res. No. 26-09 first reading by Hopper, seconded by Gibson Votes: Ayes - Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan Motion passes: 8-0 Motion to suspend the rules through second reading for Res. No. 26-09 by Hopper, seconded by Gibson Votes: Ayes - Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell Motion passes: 8-0 Motion to pass Res. No. 26-09 second reading by Gibson, seconded by Moan Votes: Ayes - Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson Motion passes: 8-0 C. Second Reading ORDINANCE NO. 26-29 AN ORDINANCE OF THE COMMON COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA, AUTHORIZING AND ESTABLISHING THE BOUNDARIES OF FOUR MUNICIPAL RIVERFRONT DEVELOPMENT PROJECT AREAS WITHIN THE CITY OF GREENWOOD PURSUANT TO INDIANA CODE §7.1-3-20-16 AND INDIANA CODE §7.1-3-20-16.1 (Sponsored by Hill, Manship) Public Hearing Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-29 second reading by Kasch, seconded by Hoggatt Votes: Ayes –Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson, Hill Motion passes: 8-0 D. NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING RESOLUTION NO. 26-10 A RESOLUTION OF THE GREENWOOD COMMON COUNCIL TERMINATING REAL PROPERTY TAX ABATEMENT FOR GREENWOOD BTS, LLC (482 Chaney Avenue) (Sponsor Campbell and Hopper) Motion to postpone Ord. No. 26-10 by Hoggatt, seconded by Hopper Votes: Ayes - Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson Nays- Hill Motion passes: 7-1 VI. New Business – Introductions of New Ordinances and Resolutions VII. Miscellaneous Business A. Public Comments This timeslot is for residents who would like to address the Council about matters not on the agenda. All materials presented at a public meeting are considered part of the official record; please provide a copy to the Clerk. Individuals- 5-minute time limit; Groups- 20-minute time limit. B. Council C. Other Miscellaneous A. Corporation Counsel B. Controller C. Mayor VIII. Adjournment In accordance with the American with Disabilities Act, the City of Greenwood is required to provide reasonable accommodations to persons with disabilities wishing to attend public meetings. Accommodations are available upon request to persons with disabilities who require alternately formatted materials, auxiliary aids, or reasonable modifications to policies and procedures to ensure effective communication and access to the public meeting. If you require accommodations to attend the meeting, please contact Public Access ADA Coordinator, Mr. Kevin Steinmetz at, 300 S. Madison Avenue, Greenwood, Indiana 46142, Tel: (317) 887-5000, steinmek@greenwood.in.gov or contact Telecommunications Relay Services (TRS) at 711 to relay your request to Public Access ADA Coordinator. Please allow at least two business days to arrange for accommodations. The Mission of the Beech Grove Parks Board is to create and responsibly manage a citywide system of parks, open space, and cultural resources, and to provide recreational, cultural, and educational programs based on these resources to enhance the quality of life for all Beech Grove citizens.
Meetings The Board of Parks and Recreation meets at 7:00pm on the second Wednesday of the month. beech grove common council
The Beech Grove Common Council is comprised of seven members elected to four-year terms; two at-large and five elected from the five Council districts. The Council is the legislative body of the city. It adopts the annual budget for the city, appropriates tax monies, passes city ordinances and resolutions, and makes appointments to certain boards and commissions. Regular meetings of the Com mon Council are held at 7:00 p.m. on the first Monday of each month. In the event the regular meeting day falls on a legal holiday, the meeting will be held the day following the holiday. Special meetings may called by the Mayor with at least three days notice and for a specified purpose. The Mayor, or in his or her absence the President Pro-Tempore of the Common Council, serves as presiding officer. Email the entire council at citycouncil@beechgrove.com .

New plumbing apprenticeship training center to officially open in Beech Grove, transforming longtimevacant site in the heart of the city
(Beech Grove, Ind.) Mechanical Skills, Inc. and the City of Beech Grove will celebrate the grand opening of a new plumbing apprenticeship training center on Monday, Aug. 10 , marking the completion of a project that has transformed a longtime vacant parcel into a hub for the skilled trades in the heart of the city.
Located at 1831 Albany Street, the site was once home to a Marsh and Safeway grocery store before sitting vacant for years. The new 20,000-square-foot facility now serves as a center for education and workforce development, while bringing new investment and activity to a key corridor adjacent to Main Street.

Falcon Youth Sports is an organization created to serve families of Perry Meridian elementary schools. Our goal is to present families and students with sports opportunities. We want to make it easy to get your kids involved! Why should I join Falcon Youth Sports? By joining the Facebook page or email list you will receive information about athletic opportunities for your child in a convenient way. Why should my child participate in sports? There is countless research to support the benefits of youth participating in sports. Participating in sports is associated with… ● Higher self esteem and more confidence ● Improved health ● Higher levels of academic achievement ● Improved teamwork and participation skills ● Great leadership qualities Developed by the PCSFN Science Board Here are a few sports opportunities you can look forward to this school year… Fall Winter Spring ● Football (Spring sign-ups) ● Cheer (Spring sign-ups) ● Soccer ● Run Club ● Basketball Clinics and try-outs ● Boys and Girls Basketball ● Wrestling ● Hockey ● Swimming ● Indoor Soccer ● Volleyball ● Swimming ● Basketball Clinics ● Little League Baseball & Softball ● Flag Football ● Athletic Enhancement Camp Many sports camps are oﬀered over summer break! Join the Southside Swim Team! Evaluations for the Fall Competitive Swim Team: August 28 6-7pm Southport High School (Door 8) https://www.southsideindyaquatics.com/page/home Questions? Email lcox@perryschools.org
